transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-26
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Novapay CTO), Aisha Khan (Platform Eng), Tom Lee (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): review of recent latency runs, streaming improvements help TTFT ~15-30ms, kernel mismatch on older GPUs causing p99 spikes, need kernel+quantization sweep and a staging prompt set from Novapay.

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check — audio ok?
00:05 Carlos: yeah, good here. thx.
00:08 Jordan: cool. so agenda today — quick run through the numbers from last week's bench, then priya will talk through kernel and quantization options, and we want to agree on next steps for the staging run.
00:20 Aisha: sounds good. our priority is TTFT and p99 for bursty checkout flows — customers hit spikes and it's visible in traces.
00:28 Priya: right, and we've been focusing on two things: streaming enabled vs non-streaming, and selecting optimized kernels for the sequence lengths you're seeing. initial runs showed streaming drops TTFT by about 80-120ms on average for 512 seqs, but depends on chunk size.
00:42 Tom: quick q, are those numbers with kv cache warm? meaning cold start impact?
00:46 Priya: good call — the numbers Jordan sent earlier are mixed; some runs were warm and some cold. cold TTFT was an issue — we saw 180ms to first token on cold for the Llama-like variant, warm dropped to 95-110ms.
01:02 Carlos: 180ms cold is high for our use-case, customers expect <150ms ideally. can you replicate cold-start mitigation?
01:10 Priya: there are a couple levers — model selection (smaller decoder variant), streaming chunk size (smaller chunk gives earlier first token), and kernel selection/compilation flags. on your hardware (we think it's A10s?), some kernels are suboptimal. with the compiled fused-kernel path on newer drivers we get p95 shrinkage.
01:28 Aisha: yes, our staging is a bit older — NVIDIA A10s with driver 520.x. production will be similar. we can't upgrade drivers easily right now.
01:36 Priya: okay that explains it. driver + cuBLAS/cuDNN influence kernel choice. we'll run a kernel compatibility map and pick the best codepath given your driver. in our last run, switching to the matmul-optimized kernel shaved p99 by ~40ms but increased median slightly due to different memory access patterns.
01:55 Jordan: quick note — there were some transcription errors in the sheet, ignore the row labelled 'seq 2048' — that was a mislabeled run. priya, can you explain the streaming chunk tradeoffs again?
02:06 Priya: yeah. streaming basically flushes partial tokens earlier; chunk-size is how many tokens we accumulate before emitting. smaller chunk -> earlier TTFT but increases total compute overhead and may increase total token latency slightly. for your checkout prompts (median ~80 tokens) a chunk of 8-12 hits a good balance. for longer contexts, different tuning.
02:28 Tom: how about batching? we saw in one test that larger batch sizes improved throughput but hurt TTFT a lot.
02:35 Priya: correct. batching improves throughput per GPU but introduces scheduling delay. we try autoscaling with small per-request queuing to keep per-request TTFT under SLO; Redwood's runtime can route low-latency traffic to reserved small-batch pools.
02:49 Carlos: route by policy, got it. Any risk of falling back to a larger model variant when busy and increasing latency unpredictably?
02:56 Jordan: we surfaced fallback policies — default is prefer latency; fallback to larger models is only for capacity if configured. we'll share the exact policy config we used in the POC.
03:08 Aisha: can you talk about quantization effects? we've heard int8 can sometimes add jitter on p99 for some GEMM paths.
03:14 Priya: yes. quantization reduces memory and kernel time but different kernels handle int8/int4 differently. int8 gave us 10-20% latency wins median, but on A10 with older drivers some int8 kernels fell back to less optimized codepaths causing p99 variance. int4 can be faster but has more accuracy risk. we'll run a controlled int8 vs fp16 sweep on your seq distribution.
03:38 Tom: please include raw latency histograms, not just averages. p99 matters more to us.
03:42 Priya: agreed — we'll include p50/p95/p99 and bootstrapped CI.
03:48 Jordan: we also did a small test with prefix/KV cache for repeated sessions; results were promising — up to 40% fewer compute ops after warm-up. but that's only useful if your traffic is sticky.
04:02 Aisha: our checkout flow often repeats across a session, so KV cache sounds useful. is there memory pressure or eviction behavior we should care about?
04:10 Priya: it's LRU-ish; you can size the cache per-instance. big sessions can cause eviction and extra latency if your average session length is high. we'll recommend cache size and eviction policy based on your session profile once you share prompt set.
04:24 Carlos: what's the expected improvement if we do everything — driver updates, kernel picks, streaming, smaller chunking? can we get cold TTFT under 120ms?
04:33 Priya: with driver upgrade + compiled kernels + streaming small chunk we hit ~95-110ms on cold in a controlled run. without driver updates, probably 120-150ms depending on kernel availability.
04:45 Jordan: note that driver upgrades may require maintenance windows for you; if that's a blocker we'll prioritize kernel workarounds and streaming which don't need infra changes.
04:55 Tom: for our timeline — we want to finish validation in 2 weeks and decide on Dedicated vs Hosted. cost will matter. can you include cost delta for reserved small-batch pool vs shared hosted?
05:05 Jordan: yes — I'll add a cost sheet. rough numbers show small-batch reserved capacity is about 1.3x cost but gives 30-40% better median latency and far better tail under bursty load.
05:18 Aisha: what about SLO for streaming? any stability concerns with partial tokens in our downstream consumer?
05:24 Priya: streaming is safe — we guarantee finalization tokens and Redwood supports function-calling and delimited outputs. only thing is if your consumer can't handle incremental output we keep chunking larger.
05:36 Carlos: ok, let's talk ops: we need audit logs, KMS integration, and RBAC before we can move to Private or Dedicated. is that on your roadmap?
05:45 Jordan: yes, Private supports KMS/HSM and RBAC; we'll share the security doc. for POC we'll keep things in staging but we can enable logs and SSO for audit.
05:56 Tom: any blockers from Redwood side to run the kernel sweep on our staging?
06:00 Priya: just SSH access to staging nodes or similar read-only metrics and the prompt set. we don't need keys to production. ideally a staging key and a small fleet with the same drivers and GPU type.
06:12 Carlos: okay we'll provision that; tom can follow up.
06:16 (background cross-talk)
06:20 Jordan: quick pause — real world note, we also saw a regression when sequence length spiked to 1024 — the matmul path behaved different and p99 jumped. priya, did we capture which kernel had that regression?
06:33 Priya: yes — that was the fallback GEMM kernel that handles large sequences; when seq length distribution shifts, the runtime switches path and we saw a memory-copy increase. the plan is to pin optimal kernels for the expected distribution or use runtime heuristics to avoid the fallback during bursts.
06:49 Tom: can heuristics be toggled at runtime? we may want to default to safer path during peak hours.
06:55 Priya: yes, they can be toggled per-route. that's part of the rollout config — canary, A/B, and immediate revert.
07:06 Jordan: ok wrapping up — let's recap actions and timeline. I'll share the perf spreadsheet and cost delta by 5/28. Priya to run kernel/quant sweep and return logs by 6/1. Novapay to provide staging prompt set and enable access by 5/31. We'll do a 30m follow-up bench on 6/2 to validate streaming changes. Anything else?
07:29 Carlos: nope that's it. thanks all.
07:33 Aisha: thanks.
07:35 Jordan: thanks everyone — talk soon. bye.

End of transcript.
